11	In `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics`, `git status` on a fresh Windows checkout lists nearly every tracked file as modified — typically 57 files. **It is not a content change.** The working tree holds CRLF, the blobs hold LF. `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` returns empty. There is no `.gitattributes` and `core.autocrlf` is unset.
12	
13	**Why:** the repo is edited on Windows by a host editor that writes CRLF, but git stored LF. Without attributes or config, every file reads as dirty, which buries the handful of real changes and invites a panic or a mass "fix" commit.
14	
15	**How to apply:**
16	- Always run `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol --stat` before believing a diff stat in this repo.
17	- Before committing, stage only the files you actually changed. Never `git add -A`.
18	- If the Edit/Write tool round-trips a file, it may convert it to CRLF. This happened during chat-3: a 2-line fix became 1,248 changed lines. Caught it with `--ignore-cr-at-eol`, reset the commit, normalised the file back to LF with `bytes.replace(b'\r\n', b'\n')`, and recommitted so it showed 420 insertions / 2 deletions.
19	- If a commit already contains EOL churn, `git reset --soft HEAD~1`, normalise, re-stage the specific paths, recommit.
20	- Removing stale `.git/*.lock` files on this mount needs `mcp__cowork__allow_cowork_file_delete` first — `rm` fails with "Operation not permitted" otherwise, and a leftover `index.lock` blocks all git writes.
21	
22	Consider adding a `.gitattributes` with `* text=auto eol=lf` if the owner wants this gone permanently — but that is a repo-wide change and should be asked about, not done unilaterally.
23

15	**Contents, eight parts plus an appendix:** the product and why physics rather than ML; the six models; Stage 0–8 across every commit with every correction (Stage 8 is chat-4 — the replication series and the model decision; Stage 11 is chat-7 — collector credentials, the gate that was added after the write it guarded, and the key directory's consistency-not-signature reasoning); the 38-artifact docket document by document plus the D00 Part IV precedence ladder; the loss of chat-1's work and its mechanism; what chat-2 rebuilt; internal strategy in `assets/`; open items, with Findings 1 and 2 recorded as CLOSED and the reasoning kept; how to resume; appendix with repository map, commit chronology and status table.

And a `TableOfContents` field renders empty in LibreOffice/`soffice` conversion because nothing updates the field, so the document carries a static "Parts" table as well; keep both.
18	
19	**Second class of gotcha, found at chat-4's close:** `P()` writes one TextRun, so `**bold**` and backtick-code written into a paragraph render as literal asterisks/backticks. `PB()` and `inlineRuns()` now split on `**` and backticks. Two ways to break it: hand a runs array where a `Paragraph` is expected (document.xml gets `<0/>`, and LibreOffice says "source file could not be loaded"), or wrap the runs in an extra array (text vanishes silently with no error).

That pass caught both original defects plus a dark empty header band on the cover table. Cheaper checks that catch most regressions: `pdfinfo | grep -i pages` for page count, and `pdftotext | grep -c '\*\*'` for unconverted markdown.

10	
11	A new test file in AxiomDynamics is verified by **its own per-file PASS count**,
12	never by the suite total moving. `tests/run_tests.py` imports each module and
13	calls `main()`; a file written without the `@test` decorator or without
14	`main()` prints its section header and runs nothing, and the aggregate can still
15	appear to rise because the count comes from somewhere else.
16	
17	**Why:** in chat-7, `test_ingest_auth.py` and `test_key_directory.py` were
18	first written without `main()`. The suite reported `340 passed, 0 failed` while
19	zero of those 30 tests had executed, and two commit messages quoted the
20	inflated number. It was caught by looking at the per-file output, not the exit
21	status — the exit status was green.
22	
23	**How to apply:** after adding a test file, run `python3 -I tests/<file>.py`
24	alone and read the last line; then confirm the new file's name appears in the
25	full runner's output with a plausible PASS count. Treat a suite total that jumps
26	by an amount larger than the number of `@test` functions you actually wrote as a
27	signal to stop and look. Same family as the vacuous ledger test, the
28	self-referential ROI test, and the inert guard: a green number that means less
29	than it appears to.

1	# Chat-8 — Carry-Forward
2	
3	**State at rollover:** suite **359 passed, 0 failed**. Nothing outstanding — the
4	owner pushed through `PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat` during the chat and `origin/main`
5	moved to the last chat-8 commit by `update by push`. Verify with
6	`git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD`; **no hash is written here**, because any
7	hash in a file is stale the moment it is committed.
8	
9	Chat-8 closed chat-7's four surviving mutations and wrote the AD-2 key custody
10	procedure. Between them those two jobs found **five defects that a green suite of
11	346 tests had not found** — two in the mutation driver, three in the product.
12	
13	---
14	
15	## Read in this order
16	
17	1. `project-logs/CURRENT-STATE.md`
18	2. This file
19	3. `project-logs/chat-8/SUMMARY.md`
20	4. `assets/mutation-survivors-closed-2026-11-11.md` (phase one)
21	5. `assets/key-custody-procedure-2026-11-11.md` (phase two)
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Phase one — the four mutation survivors
26	
27	Commit **`a4ccc0b`**. Driver now reports **18 mutations, 18 killed, 0 survived**.
28	Suite 346 → 351.
29	
30	| # | What was missing | Test added |
31	|---|---|---|
32	| M2 | No test compared the **error text**; only status and row count | `test_the_http_route_refuses_a_missing_or_bad_token_and_logs_nothing` asserts `"collector enrollment" in body["error"]` |
33	| M3 | Garbage body **with an unknown token** — the one shape where a row reaches the ingest log while the status stays 401 | `test_ingest_with_an_unknown_token_is_401_and_logs_nothing` |
34	| M5 | Nothing called the route function directly with `headers={}` | `test_the_route_refuses_a_missing_header_when_a_collector_is_enrolled` |
35	| M9 | The forged-append test tripped the **prev_hash** check, never the entry-hash check | `test_a_row_with_the_right_prev_hash_but_a_wrong_entry_hash_is_caught` |
36	
37	**M2 was not the gap it was reported to be.** I first declared it an equivalent
38	mutant; an independent audit found the 401 *text* differs. I had compared status
39	and side effects and stopped there.
40	
41	### Two defects in the driver, both of which would have produced false greens
42	
43	- **An `EQUIVALENT` table keyed by mutation index.** The auditor substituted a
44	  genuine survivor into that slot and the driver printed "equivalent" and exited
45	  **0**. It would have absorbed any real survivor landing there. Removed
46	  entirely; a survivor now always prints `ALIVE`, with instructions to decide by
47	  reading the code and an explicit prohibition on index-keyed exemptions.
48	- **Pycache isolation was inert.** The suite runs under `-I`, and **`-I` sets
49	  `sys.pycache_prefix` to `None`**, discarding `PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX`. Bytecode
50	  still reached the source tree. Now `-X pycache_prefix=<fresh tmp dir>`, which
51	  `-I` honours. Both claims verified empirically, both ways.
52	
53	The driver also now removes a stale snapshot before writing one (a leftover
54	snapshot from an interrupted run would restore a *mutated* tree).
55	
56	---
57	
58	## Phase two — the AD-2 custody procedure (D09 §8.4)
59	
60	Commit **`3de44cf`**; record corrections `1f1fce8`. Suite 351 → 359.
61	
62	Eight subsections, placed in D09 beside §4.5 which already does the same job for
63	the export key — no new document, no new docket ID. 8.4.1 separates the three
64	credentials; 8.4.2–8.4.5 are joiner, mover, leaver, rotation in dependency order;
65	8.4.6 is the custody log (`key_id`, never the key); 8.4.7 forbids interchange
66	with the export key; 8.4.8 states the limits.
67	
68	### Three product defects the procedure exposed, none found by a test
69	
70	1. **A key could be registered to a second reviewer, and the second one won.**
71	   `register` refused only a key revoked *anywhere* in history. A *live* key
72	   presented under a different reviewer was accepted, and because `attest`
73	   resolves the **newest** entry for a `key_id` — deliberately, so renewal works
74	   — the second reviewer took the key over and the original holder was locked
75	   out of their own key. The register is append-only, so the bad binding could
76	   never be removed; `entries_consistent` caught it only at publish time.
77	   Now refused **at the write**. A renewal under a new certificate for the
78	   **same** reviewer still works — my first fix refused that too and would have
79	   broken rotation to fix sharing.
80	2. **A refused key directory still handed back bindings** — `{"ok": False,
81	   "bindings": {"<key>": "Hoffman"}}` for the directory it had just refused.
82	   Now `{}` on refusal.
83	3. **The procedure named a step nobody could perform.** The only code that made
84	   a reviewer key was `seed_demo_account.py`, which generates one and discards
85	   it. `tools/issue_reviewer_key.py` is the joiner step: generate, register,
86	   print the `key_id`, never the key, refuse to overwrite an existing key file.
87	
88	Every mechanism claim in §8.4 was **executed** rather than reasoned about. Both
89	new guards are mutation-tested — each fails exactly one test when removed, and no
90	other. One more defect, in my own writing: the phase-two record put the B01 AD-2
91	bullet at "§10". B01 has no §10; the bullet sits in the unnumbered preamble.
92	Corrected before it was committed.
93	
94	---
95	
96	## Next ladder — low to high, one at a time
97	
98	Both items below were offered at chat-8's close and neither is started.
99	
100	1. **Regenerate the build-history docx for chat-8** *(low)*.
101	   `project-logs/build-history-summary.js` has stages 1–11; chat-8 is stage 12.
102	   The close gate asserts `Stage 11` is present, so that assertion must become
103	   `Stage 12` in the same edit or it will pin the document to a stale stage.
104	   Rebuild with node, then check: no literal `**` or backticks in the extracted
105	   text, and render to PDF and read the pages — the TOC field renders empty in
106	   converters that do not update fields.
107	2. **Attestation at entry** *(medium)*. Entry now requires a live session; it
108	   does not require an attestation, so an unattested row is still possible. This
109	   changes `POST /api/warrant/<id>/disposition` and its tests. It does **not**
110	   close item 1 — a key holder is not a person.
111	3. **The real payload schema** *(medium, blocked on the Railroad)*. Item 5's
112	   authentication half closed in chat-7; the schema must be agreed with them
113	   before it can be written.
114	4. **Apply the supply-chain tools** *(high, Q1–Q2 2027 targets)*. SBOM, hash
115	   pinning and GPG signing are **built, not applied**. Applying them is a
116	   release-process change, not a code change.
117	5. **D07 §14.5 — governing law, seat and forum** *(counsel, not engineering)*.
118	   Blocks first execution.
119	
120	---
121	
122	## Standing instructions, unchanged
123	
124	- All project work written **directly into `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics`**, first
125	  pass, committed in the same pass. No drafts in the sandbox — a whole phase was
126	  lost that way.
127	- **Verify against the file, then write.** Never cite from memory.
128	- **125K tokens per chat.** At the cap, alert and roll over.
129	- **Every build phase opens with a low→high priority ladder**, worked one item at

292	`AxiomDynamics-ROI-Calculator.xlsx` in the docket is now the corrected file —

298	## Transcript — chat-4 extracted and committed at close, 2026-11-10

302	5,667 events, 12 MB, into

308	wrote a hard-coded `"# Chat-3"` heading into every extract regardless of which
309	session it was processing, so chat-4's file opened under the wrong title. It now

313	**Build history regenerated at 39 pages (chat-6).** Stage 10 was added for
314	chat-6 — authenticated disposition entry and the inert guard the audit found —
315	and Part VII's two entry-gating rows were rewritten rather than left to contradict
316	the code. The paragraph below records the chat-5 revision. Stage 9 was added for
317	chat-5 — the ledger audit, the ingest path, the supply-chain tools and
318	attribution — and Part VII's gap register was rebuilt rather than patched: the
319	ingest row, the attribution row and the supply-chain rows all described states
320	that chat-5 changed, and three of them had drifted into claiming more than the
321	code did. The earlier revision, at chat-4's close, is recorded above: Part VII

327	## Signed ledger export — built 2026-11-10 (AD-3 part two), commit `d9c83d4`
328	
329	`backend/ledger_export.py` builds an HMAC-SHA256-signed bundle: manifest (id
330	range, record count, head hash, the ledger's own head, covered-field list,
331	canonicalisation rule, chain status, previous bundle digest), every record in
332	canonical form, and a signature over the whole. `tools/verify_ledger_export.py`

336	
337	**Why HMAC and not Ed25519:** the stdlib has no asymmetric primitive, and
338	hand-rolling one in a product that tells CISOs it does not hand-roll crypto
339	would be worse than the gap. The two limits — cannot name the signer, cannot
340	date itself — are stated in B01 §4.5a rather than footnoted.
341	
342	**The audit caught a serious hole, and this is the part worth remembering.**
343	The first version let a total wipe verify green: delete every row, export
344	honestly, and a recipient holding the previous bundle was told everything
345	passed. Each check was individually correct; none compared the bundle against
346	one already held. Fixed by recording the ledger's own head in every bundle and
347	failing when a later bundle reports a shorter ledger (`no_truncation`), plus
348	`genesis_anchor` for rows deleted from the front. Export tests are now 43; the
349	suite at the time of that build was 80. Three tests assert a failure to detect on purpose, recording disclosed
350	limits rather than hiding them.

352	**What it does not do:** detect a ledger wiped before the first bundle in a
353	series; replicate off-box on a schedule; name the signer. D09 §4.5 makes bundle
354	retention and a written key-custody procedure the controls that carry that

356	
357	Internal account: `assets/ledger-export-build-2026-11-09.md`.

377	The gap that had been disclosed in six documents since `cf2e6ba` is closed at

379	
380	- `backend/store.py` rewritten. Records are inserted, never updated. A second
381	  decision on an advisory is a new row carrying `supersedes_id`; the earlier row
382	  keeps its content and timestamp. `BEFORE UPDATE` and `BEFORE DELETE` triggers
383	  `RAISE(ABORT)`, so the guarantee lives in the schema rather than in convention.
384	  Every row stores `prev_hash` and `record_hash` — a SHA-256 over its own
385	  canonical content plus the predecessor's hash — and `verify_chain()`
386	  recomputes the whole chain and names the first row that fails.
387	- Migration from the v1 one-row-per-advisory table runs inside `init_db()`,
388	  preserves the surviving decision and its original timestamp, and does not
389	  fabricate history that the old schema had already destroyed.
390	- 17 adversarial tests in `tests/test_store.py`: an UPDATE, a DELETE, a second
391	  disposition, a tampered row, a removed row, and two migration shapes. Each
392	  asserts the attempt fails or is detected. `tests/run_tests.py` now discovers
393	  every `test_*.py`, so the total suite is 38.
394	- New routes: `GET /api/warrant/{id}/disposition` (full trail, with `chain_ok`)
395	  and `GET /api/ledger/verify`. The dashboard shows the decision trail under the
396	  form and marks a corrected decision as superseding an earlier record.
397	
398	**What it does not prove, and the docket now says so in these words:** the chain
399	is tamper-*evident*, not tamper-*proof*. A party with write access to the
400	database file can drop the triggers, rewrite rows and recompute every hash. That
401	is why items 6 and 8 above stay open.
402	
403	Docket corrected in the same commit: B01 §4 and §7 items 2/8, D09 §4.4 and the
404	audit-logging row, F09 Part 6 and Part 7, F00, B02, C02, D12, D14 §5, D00 Part V
405	and Part VI, and the root README.

407	## A1 builder — fixed in chat-3
408	
409	Two defects in `A1-ROI-MODEL/build_roi_calculator.py`, both cosmetic to the
410	workbook but both real if anyone runs it:
411	
412	- The sheet-5 assumptions note attributed a **2% catastrophic escalation rate** to
413	  a model whose cell B17 has held **0.05%** since the correction. A reader
414	  reconciling the sheet against its own footnote would find a ten-fold conflict.
415	- The script saved to `/sessions/.../mnt/outputs/...`, a path inside the destroyed
416	  chat-1 sandbox, so running it raised `FileNotFoundError`. It now writes beside
417	  itself.

419	
420	## Git state
421	
422	The sandbox **cannot reach GitHub** — `git push` and `git fetch` both fail with
423	HTTP 403 from the proxy. Its `origin/main` ref therefore only advances when the
424	owner pushes and the sandbox is told the result. Do not trust it as evidence of
425	remote state without checking the commits page.
426	
427	**Pushing is done by the owner**, with `PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat` in the repo root. It
428	prints the commits waiting to go up and verifies afterwards.
429	
430	**Last confirmed pushed state, 2026-11-10:** the owner's push moved the remote to
431	`bb99cdd`. Everything after it is local and waiting, and every edit to this file
432	adds to the queue — so the count is deliberately not written here. Run
433	`git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD`.
434	
435	**The host repo at `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics` is authoritative for push state.**
436	Verify by opening the commits page.
437	
438	**The line-ending trap.** `git status` in this repo lists nearly every tracked file
439	as modified on a fresh Windows checkout. It is CRLF working-tree content against
440	LF blobs, not a content change — `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` returns empty.
441	There is no `.gitattributes` and `core.autocrlf` is unset. **Always check with
442	`--ignore-cr-at-eol` before believing a diff stat**, and never let an editor
443	rewrite a whole file's endings into a commit: doing so once during chat-3 turned a
444	two-line fix into 1,248 changed lines, which had to be reset and recommitted.
445	
446	
447	## What was lost in the chat-1 → chat-2 transition
448	
449	Recorded here so nobody goes looking for it:
450	
451	- Three commits built at the end of chat-1 (`0b66d21`, `cb4f74d`, and the
452	  F00/D07/Q6 work) existed only in the old sandbox. **`F00` Rule 7, the D07 §14
453	  rewrite and Q6 were rebuilt into the repository in chat-2.** The project-logs
454	  structure was rebuilt. The transcripts were not and cannot be — see
455	  `README.md`.
456	- Because the rebuild is a reconstruction rather than a recovery, the wording may
457	  differ from what chat-1 wrote. The *decisions* are identical; the prose is not
458	  guaranteed to be. Do not treat the current text as a restoration of an earlier
459	  draft.
460	
461	## Standing instructions
462	
463	- **[WORK LOCATION] All project work is written directly into this repository, first pass, and committed in the same pass.** No drafts in sandbox scratch space — that is how chat-1's final phase was lost.
464	- Keep the same concept throughout — consistency of framing across every document.
465	- Internal analysis goes in `assets/`, never `client-assets/`.
466	- Verify against the file before writing the claim.
467	
468	## Why chat-1's work was lost — the mechanism
469	
470	Not a deletion. The work was never on the owner's machine.
471	
472	Chat-1 built the repo inside a temporary sandbox container. To get anything out
473	it bundled the repo, embedded the bundle in a `.bat`, and the owner ran it once —
474	which is how `de9b245` reached GitHub. **Everything chat-1 did after that push
475	stayed in the container**, including the F00 Rule 7 work, the D07 §14 rewrite, Q6
476	and the transcripts. The bundle was never remade. When the session ended the
477	container was destroyed and took all of it.
478	
479	The failure was treating "committed" as "safe." Inside that container it only
480	meant "saved somewhere that is about to be emptied."
481	
482	**The rule that follows:** there is no automatic export. A commit in the sandbox
483	is not durable until it is in `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics` and pushed. Never tell
484	the owner work is saved without saying where it physically is.

# AxiomDynamics — Current State

**Last updated:** 2026-11-11 (**chat-8 in progress** — chat-7's four mutation
survivors closed and the AD-2 custody procedure written; the driver reports
**18 mutations, 18 killed, 0 survived**, suite **359**). Next session: read
`CURRENT-STATE.md`, then the latest `chat-N/CARRY-FORWARD.md`. Accounts:
`assets/mutation-survivors-closed-2026-11-11.md` (phase one),
`assets/key-custody-procedure-2026-11-11.md` (phase two).
**Repository:** `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics`
**Remote:** `github.com/kaanju19-lang/AxiomDynamics` (private)
**Push state:** `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD` is the only answer that
counts. As last confirmed the local remote-tracking ref stood at `bb99cdd`; the
first commit after it is `893096e`. Never trust a hash written in this file
— check with git, because this file's own commit moves the top of the branch
every time it is edited. Run `PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat` in the repo root. The sandbox
cannot reach GitHub: `git push` and `git fetch` both fail with HTTP 403 from the
proxy, so a local `origin/main` ref is not proof of what the remote holds.

---

## Chat-6 build — authenticated disposition entry (AD-2 entry half), 2026-11-11

**Built and committed in chat-6: commits `db569a4` and `83010d0`. Suite
238 → 315, all green. Not yet pushed.** Full account:
`assets/session-entry-build-2026-11-11.md`.

The gap chat-5 left: `POST /api/warrant/<id>/disposition` read `reviewer_name`
and `cert_id` out of the request body, so the name on a decision was a claim even
though the registry could verify one after the fact. `backend/accounts.py` now
binds an account to a live certification record and gates entry on a bearer
token; identity comes from the resolved session and a body carrying either field
is **refused**. `resolve_session` re-checks the certificate, and a second check
runs inside the ledger's write transaction so a revocation landing between
resolve and INSERT cannot record a decision. With no account enrolled the path is
**closed (503)** rather than reopened to free text. `tools/seed_demo_account.py`
is the deliberate act that opens it. The frontend now signs in; the reviewer and
certification boxes are gone because they would be a lie about what the row says.

**The audit is the part worth reading.** An independent agent told to *falsify*
the claim found the transaction guard **inert** — it *returned* a boolean and the
caller discarded it, so a certificate revoked in the resolve-to-INSERT window
still produced HTTP 200 and a row. 310 tests were green. They missed it because
the test simulated the race with a guard that *raised*, which is not the guard
the route installs. A guard whose only tested failure mode is one the caller does
not use is not a guard — the same shape as the vacuous ledger and ROI tests.
Fixed, with the exploit reproduced verbatim against the fix's removal.

Also fixed from the hostile-input sweep: two 500s on malformed bodies
(`note` as an object, `disposition` as a list).

Still open: **key custody and joiner/mover/leaver** (a written procedure), a
**signed key directory**, and requiring an **attestation** at entry as well as a
session. Entry proves a credential was presented; it does not prove a person.

## Chat-8 phase one — the four mutation survivors are closed, 2026-11-11

Commit `a4ccc0b`. **Driver: 18 mutations, 18 killed, 0 survived. Suite 346 → 351.**
Account: `assets/mutation-survivors-closed-2026-11-11.md`.

M5 and M9 were the straightforward coverage gaps the carry-forward described.
M3 needed a case nothing had: a garbage body **plus an unknown token** — with
the resolve failure swallowed, that is the one shape where a row reaches the
ingest log while the status stays 401. **M2 was not the gap it was reported to
be**; I first decided it was an equivalent mutant and was wrong, because the
status and the row count match but the **error text does not**. The test now
asserts the message.

**Two defects in the driver itself were found by an independent audit after
every mutation was green**, and both matter more than the tests:

- An `EQUIVALENT` table I added was keyed by mutation **index**. The auditor
  put a genuine survivor in that slot and the driver printed "equivalent" and
  exited **0**. It would have absorbed any real survivor landing there.
  Removed; a survivor now always prints `ALIVE`.
- The pycache isolation was **inert**: the suite runs under `-I`, and `-I`
  sets `sys.pycache_prefix` to `None`, discarding `PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX`.
  Bytecode still reached the source tree. Now `-X pycache_prefix=...`, which
  `-I` honours — both claims verified rather than assumed.

**Importing `backend.main` runs `store.init_db()`** against the repo root, so a
test that imports it before setting `AXIOM_DB_PATH` creates an `axiom.db` there
and dies with `disk I/O error` on this mount. `tests/test_ingest_auth.py` now
sets it first.

**`project-logs/close-gate.sh` carries chat-7's session path** and will fail
from any other session. Fix its paths before chat-8 closes.

## Chat-8 phase two — the AD-2 custody procedure, 2026-11-11

Commit `3de44cf`. B01 §7 item 1 has been open on "key custody and
joiner/mover/leaver — a written procedure, not code" since chat-6. It is now
**D09 §8.4**, eight subsections, beside §4.5 which already does the same job for
the export key. Account: `assets/key-custody-procedure-2026-11-11.md`.
**Suite 351 → 359.**

**Writing the procedure down exposed three things the code did not support, and
no test found any of them.** That is the part worth carrying:

- **A key could be registered to a second reviewer, and the second one won.**
  `register` refused only a key revoked *anywhere* in its history; a *live* key
  presented under a different reviewer was accepted, and because `attest`
  resolves the newest entry for a `key_id` — deliberately, so renewal works —
  the second reviewer took the key over and the original holder was locked out
  of their own key. The register is append-only, so the binding could never be
  removed. Now refused at the write. A renewal under a new certificate for the
  **same** reviewer still works; my first attempt refused that too and would
  have broken rotation to fix sharing.
- **A refused key directory still handed back bindings** — `ok=False` alongside
  `bindings={'<key>': 'Hoffman'}` for the directory it had just refused. Now
  `{}`.
- **The procedure named a step nobody could perform.** The only code that made
  a reviewer key was `seed_demo_account.py`, which generates one and discards
  it. `tools/issue_reviewer_key.py` is the joiner step: generate, register,
  print the `key_id`, never the key, refuse to overwrite an existing key file.

Every mechanism claim in §8.4 was executed rather than reasoned about. Both new
guards are mutation-tested — each fails exactly one test when removed.
**Item 1 is not closed:** a credential holder is not a person, the HMAC scheme
is symmetric, a demo cannot attest, and every step but revocation is performed
by a human. What changed is that the item is now auditable under D09 §10.1, and
B01 §7 item 1 says that rather than implying a document settles it.

## What this project is

Physics-first predictive maintenance for freight rail. Six named physical models
— thermodynamics with per-axle rolling z-score, peer median/MAD comparison,
kinematics, acoustics (BPFO/BPFI/BSF/FTF), same-axle left/right differential, and
an executive ROI panel — instead of black-box ML or fixed alarm thresholds.

The Master Brief Docket is in `client-assets/MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/`: 38 artifacts
— 36 Markdown documents, the A1 Excel model (with its build script beside it) and
the B03 HTML infographic — across A (commercial), B (technical), C (deployment)
and D (contractual) series plus F (forms).

## Build status

**38 artifacts on disk; 37 docket IDs on disk (A1 is a folder holding the `.xlsx`
and the builder, so it counts as one ID and two files).** The docket index (D00)
carries 37 ID rows; 34 are marked `**Built**` in bold, and B02 (.md) and B03
(.html) carry plain "Built" with a format qualifier. D00 Part IV is the authority
on status, not this file.

A long-form account of the whole build — every stage, every document, every
correction, and the loss and rebuild — is at
`project-logs/AxiomDynamics-Build-History-and-Working-Summary.docx` (39 pages,
revised 2026-11-11 to carry chat-6). It is generated by
`project-logs/build-history-summary.js`; re-run
`node project-logs/build-history-summary.js` after a material change.

Open docket items are tracked in **D00 Part IV** — that table is the authority,
not this file.

## The largest known gap

**The ingest chain is built; nothing downstream is wired to it.** As of
2026-11-11 `POST /api/ingest` accepts a payload and applies schema → timestamp →
plausibility in that order: accepted for scoring (202), retained as suspect
without scoring (200), or refused with a named reason and logged (422). 24
tests. No outcome other than `accepted` emits an advisory.

Three parts remain open, disclosed in B01 §7 item 5 and B02 §2: the payload
schema is a **demonstration schema** (`axiom-detector-payload/v1`) and the real one
must be agreed with the Railroad; **the endpoint has no authentication**, which
makes it a data-poisoning route until AD-2 lands and is why it belongs on a
trusted segment; and **the demonstration fleet still scores synthetic traces** —
an accepted payload is validated and logged, not scored.

Every demonstration number therefore still demonstrates **the method**, not the
Railroad's data.

## Open items, in priority order

1. **D07 §14.5 — governing law and venue.** An open counsel decision, correctly
   labelled as open as of chat-2 (previously a blank pointing at an Order field
   that does not exist). Must be closed by signed addendum before first execution.
2. **Session-bound disposition entry, export-key identity and off-box carriage**
   — the signed export landed 2026-11-09, the **series build landed 2026-11-10**,
   and **per-disposition attribution landed 2026-11-11**
   (`backend/attribution.py`: append-only,
   **hash-chained** reviewer registry, HMAC attestations over each row's
   `record_hash` carried inside exported records, checked by both verifiers).
   What that closes: a bundle can now say which *registered reviewer key*
   attested a row, and a recipient can verify it. What remains: the *export*
   signature is still symmetric, so a bundle names no export signer;
   attribution is about a key holder, not a person, and a recipient given no
   reviewer key cannot tell an honest attestation from a fabricated one; entry
   is now gated on a **live session** but not on an attestation, so an attested
   row is still the reviewer's choice; nothing proves when a bundle was made; a ledger wiped
   before the first bundle in a series stays invisible; and **nothing carries
   the produced series off the box** — deliberate, because D09 §3.2 promises no
   outbound network, so carriage is the Railroad's physical step under §3.3.
   D09 §4.4–4.5, B01 §4.5a and §7 items 1 and 11–12. **Attribution and
   session-bound entry are no longer AD-2 dependencies; export-key identity,
   key custody and joiner/mover/leaver still are.**
   An independent adversarial audit found nine defects in this build after the
   suite was green — the worst of them let a registered key relabel another
   reviewer's row and pass both verifiers. 40 mutations, 40 killed. See
   `assets/attribution-build-2026-11-11.md`.
3. **D09 §4.4 supply-chain gaps** — SBOM (Q1 2027), hash verification of
   dependency downloads (Q1 2027), GPG-signed releases (Q2 2027). All three now
   have **tools built 2026-11-11**; none is **applied**, and D09 §4.4 carries the
   three-state distinction per control.

## Model decision — A1 governs, decided 2026-11-10 (chat-4)

The owner delegated the choice ("you decide"). **A1 governs the commercial
numbers, expressed as Option D in `assets/a2-d08-model-decision-2026-11-09.md`**:
0.05% escalation probability, $500,000 typical contained cost, $1.0B catastrophic.

What changed in the docket, all on 2026-11-10:

- **A2 §3.2 and D08 §3** anchors restated from the withdrawn 2.0x/4.1x to
  **1.77x at 500 axles, 3.36x at 10,000**, with the cost basis stated in the text
  instead of left to inference. The pilot year is charged in full and credited with
  no benefit in that calculation — the conservative frame.
- **D08 §5 restated** from A1: pilot year at the **200 axles §2 actually scopes**
  ($278,670 modelled benefit, **0.75x** the $370,000 fee — the pilot does not pay
  for itself and the document now says so); production years at 500 axles
  ($696,675/yr); four-year return **2.01x**.
- **D08 §6 restated**: six-year return **2.06x**. Close to flat against the
  four-year figure, because fee escalation from Year 4 offsets the dilution of one
  weak pilot year across more production years. It does **not** fall.
- **`backend/roi.py`** corrected: `P_CATASTROPHIC_GIVEN_MISSED_DEFECT` 2% → 0.05%,
  and the per-missed-defect value now blends the **$500,000 typical** cost rather
  than the $9.25M midpoint of the two NTSB severe benchmarks. Expected cost per
  missed defect is now **$999,750**, identical to A1's B22; the 29x overstatement is
  gone. The severe benchmarks survive as `SEVERE_FAILURE_COST_*`, explicitly
  reference-only, and the dataclass field renamed `severe_cost_range_usd` so no
  reader mistakes them for the typical case again.
- Checkers updated rather than left certifying stale text: the arithmetic pass is
  now **89 checks** and reports both findings **closed and checked**, not merely
  recorded. The decision paper's **65 checks** still reproduce (it documents the
  withdrawn figures, which is its job).

**Two things a future reader will otherwise trip over.** First, A2 §3.2 says 1.77x
at 500 axles and D08 §5 says 2.01x — different questions on the same inputs (A2
charges the pilot with no benefit; D08 credits the 200-axle pilot with its actual
benefit). A2 §3.2 now states that difference explicitly. Second, **D08 §2 scopes the
pilot at 100–200 axles**, so any pilot-year benefit computed at 500 was contradicting
the document's own scope. That defect was mine, introduced in the first restatement
and caught before commit.

## Ledger replication series — built 2026-11-10 (chat-4)

`backend/ledger_replication.py` executes the cadence D09 §4.5.4 already
specified: monthly full, weekly incremental, every bundle chained to the
previous by `previous_export_hash`, zero-record weeks kept, nothing overwritten.
`inspect` opens every bundle, recomputes its digest, verifies it against the
predecessor, and reports a missing period. 32 tests; full suite **112**.

**It deliberately does not transmit.** D09 §3.2 promises the Platform has no
outbound network, so the series accumulates in `--series-dir` on the box and
carrying it to backup media is the Railroad's step under §3.3. The owner chose
this over a network push on 2026-11-10; the reasoning is in
`assets/ledger-replication-build-2026-11-10.md`.

**Two audits found nine material defects before this was called built** — the
count is in the assets file rather than here, but the shape is worth carrying:
the release verifier rejected every full export, `inspect` could not see
tampering or gaps, the period walker hung on a 53-week ISO year, concurrent runs
duplicated bundles, and one test passed only because the check it guarded was
absent. A green suite of 108 preceded all of it.

range, record count, head hash, the ledger's own head, covered-field list,
canonicalisation rule, chain status, previous bundle digest), every record in
canonical form, and a signature over the whole. `tools/verify_ledger_export.py`
verifies it **without importing anything from `backend/`**, from an empty
directory, with `-I` — the recipient needs the bundle, the key, and a Python
standard library, nothing else.

hand-rolling one in a product that tells CISOs it does not hand-roll crypto
would be worse than the gap. The two limits — cannot name the signer, cannot
date itself — are stated in B01 §4.5a rather than footnoted.

suite at the time of that build was 80. Three tests assert a failure to detect on purpose, recording disclosed

series; replicate off-box on a schedule; name the signer. D09 §4.5 makes bundle

The sandbox **cannot reach GitHub** — `git push` and `git fetch` both fail with

as modified on a fresh Windows checkout. It is CRLF working-tree content against
LF blobs, not a content change — `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` returns empty.

## Why chat-1's work was lost — the mechanism

Not a deletion. The work was never on the owner's machine.

Chat-1 built the repo inside a temporary sandbox container. To get anything out
it bundled the repo, embedded the bundle in a `.bat`, and the owner ran it once —

is not durable until it is in `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics` and pushed. Never tell

470	Not a deletion. The work was never on the owner's machine.
471	
472	Chat-1 built the repo inside a temporary sandbox container. To get anything out
473	it bundled the repo, embedded the bundle in a `.bat`, and the owner ran it once —

478	
479	The failure was treating "committed" as "safe." Inside that container it only

483	is not durable until it is in `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics` and pushed. Never tell

203:## Part IV — Precedence and construction
204-
205-To prevent the loophole where a technical annex contradicts the master contract:
206-
207-1. **D07 Comprehensive Master Contract** governs generally.
208-2. **D02 Master Pilot Agreement** governs during the pilot term, where it conflicts with D07.
209-3. **D09 Data Processing & Security Addendum** governs on data protection and security matters.
210-4. **D03 MSA** governs structure, ordering, and change control across all orders.
211-5. **D04 SOW** governs scope of work and deliverables for that specific order.
212-6. **A2 Rate Card** governs price. **Where any document's fee differs from A2, A2 wins.**
213-7. **B-series technical annexes** are descriptive and do not create warranties unless D07 expressly incorporates them.
214-8. **F-series forms** are administrative. Where a form conflicts with an agreement, the agreement governs. A form records an event; it does not vary a term.
215-9. Where a B-series document describes a capability that D07 disclaims, **the disclaimer governs and the annex must be corrected** — this is a drafting error to be fixed, not a gap to be argued.
216-

10:- **AD-2 — Reviewer identity: local accounts plus a signed certification registry**, administered by the Railroad. No dependency on Railroad directory services, no cloud identity provider. **Built 2026-11-11 in part:** the registry is append-only and hash-chained and issues per-reviewer keys; local accounts bound to a live certification now gate disposition entry, so the identity on a row comes from the session. It remains **tamper-evident rather than signed** — registry entries carry no signature of their own — and key custody is a written procedure, not code: **now written in D09 §8.4**, covering issuance, mover, leaver, rotation and the custody log, with `tools/issue_reviewer_key.py` as the joiner step and a first-party refusal that stops one key being registered to a second reviewer. See §7 item 1.
34:| Identity & certification | **Local accounts, admin-issued credentials — operational today.** Signed certification registry: **designed, not built** (§7 item 1) | Python + SQLite |
35:| Disposition ledger | Record of reviewer decisions. **Append-only — built 2026-11-09** (§4.1, §4.6, §7 item 2) | SQLite, WAL mode; insert-only with guard triggers and SHA-256 chain |
38:| Audit export | Timestamped export with content hashes. **Not cryptographically signed** (§7 item 8) | Python |
80:2. **Authenticated identity.** A disposition is only accepted from an authenticated session bound to an issued, unexpired, unrevoked certification record. Free-text name and cert ID are not accepted. *Built 2026-11-11 — `backend/accounts.py`; the residual is the custody and joiner/mover/leaver procedure, written in D09 §8.4, which establishes who was entitled to a credential rather than who was at the keyboard. §7 item 1.*
105:**What the chain does and does not prove.** It detects a row edited in place (its own hash stops matching) and a row removed from the middle (the next row's `prev_hash` stops matching). It does **not** stop an attacker who has write access to the database file: such a party can drop the triggers, rewrite rows and recompute every hash. The chain is tamper-**evident**, not tamper-**proof**, and the difference is the reason off-box replication and signed export still matter (§7 items 6–7).
113:**What `history_continues` still does not prove, and this must stay in mind.** It checks **one anchor record** — the one the held bundle ended at. It does not compare the whole overlapping history. So a party who rewrites records the held bundle *did not* end at, and leaves that one record intact, is not caught by it; the exposure is reduced to that far narrower case rather than eliminated. Closing it properly needs a Merkle accumulator root, which is the same work as AD-2 and belongs with it (§7 item 1). **The honest sentence is: a rewrite carried out between two exports is now detectable, provided the rewritten record is the one the held bundle ended at.**
134:## 7. Production decisions required — where the code differs today
140:| 1 | Reviewer authentication | **Partly built 2026-11-11.** `backend/attribution.py` implements the certification registry: per-reviewer 32-byte keys, an append-only hash-chained registry with `BEFORE UPDATE`/`BEFORE DELETE`/`BEFORE INSERT … OR REPLACE` triggers, and HMAC attestations over each row's `record_hash` that travel inside exported records. `attest()` refuses an unregistered key, a revoked key, a key registered to a different reviewer, and a key registered under a different certificate; `register()` refuses a key revoked anywhere in its history, **and — since 2026-11-11 — a live key presented under a second reviewer**, which it previously accepted, silently transferring the key and locking its original holder out of attesting. A renewed certificate for the same reviewer may still reuse the key. Both verifiers check reviewer, certificate, registration-before-attestation and revocation-on-time, and recompute the attestation when the reviewer's key is supplied **together with the name bound to it** — a key alone cannot establish the label, because the HMAC covers the row hash and not the name. The registry is **hash-chained, not signed**: it is tamper-evident to a reader who recomputes the chain, which is weaker than authentication and is described that way everywhere it appears. **Entry is now gated 2026-11-11.** `backend/accounts.py` binds an account to a live certification record already in the registry, stores a PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 verifier (600,000 iterations, per-account salt) rather than a passphrase, and issues a bearer token of which only the SHA-256 digest is stored. `POST /api/warrant/<id>/disposition` requires that token: reviewer name and certificate ID are taken from the resolved session and **never from the request body**, and a body carrying either field is refused rather than ignored. `resolve_session` re-checks that the session is unrevoked and unexpired, that the account is live, **and that the certification behind it is still live**, so a certificate revoked mid-session stops writing immediately; a second check runs inside the ledger's own write transaction, closing the resolve-to-INSERT window. With no account enrolled the path is **closed**, not opened back up to free text. The account register is append-only and hash-chained over salt, iteration count and verifier — a swap of any of the three would hand over the account. **Established by an independent audit told to falsify it**, which found the transaction guard inert because it returned a boolean and the caller discarded it; fixed, with the exploit reproduced verbatim against the fix's removal. What this still does not do is prove a human was at the keyboard, protect the token in transit (§7 item 10), or make attestation stronger — and entry still does **not** require an attestation, only a live session | AD-2 remainder: **key custody and joiner/mover/leaver procedure** — a written process, **now written in D09 §8.4**, with issuance in `tools/issue_reviewer_key.py`. **The signed key directory is built 2026-11-11:** `backend/key_directory.py` publishes a signed list of reviewer↔key_id↔cert_id bindings (no key material), `tools/publish_key_directory.py` builds it on the Platform host and refuses if the registry chain does not verify, and `tools/verify_key_directory.py` verifies it on a recipient machine importing nothing from `backend/`. It **proves the export-key holder authored those bindings, not that they are entitled to** — the signature is symmetric — so it is portable and tamper-evident rather than authenticated. Attestation is still optional at entry |

It **proves the export-key holder authored those bindings, not that they are entitled to** — the signature is symmetric — so it is portable and tamper-evident rather than authenticated. | 3 | Timestamps | SQLite `datetime('now')` default | Server-generated with NTP-synced clock |
| 4 | Storage durability | The demonstration environment's storage is ephemeral — the demo database is lost on spin-down | Persistent volume on Railroad hardware |
| 5 | Sensor ingest | **The validation chain and collector authentication are built 2026-11-11; the payload schema is not the Railroad's.** `backend/ingest.py` implements B02 §2's three gates (schema → timestamp → plausibility) over a versioned demonstration schema, fails closed, and logs every outcome. **Ingest is now authenticated 2026-11-11.** `backend/ingest_auth.py` gives a collector its own credential, deliberately separate from a reviewer account: a collector is enrolled by name, receives a 32-byte bearer token once (only the SHA-256 digest is stored), and the registry is append-only and hash-chained. `POST /api/ingest` checks the credential **before reading or logging the body** — an earlier draft logged unparseable bodies on the way in, so any anonymous caller could append rows to the ingest log; the gate now runs first, and a missing, dead or unissued token is a 401 while a deployment with no enrolled collector is **closed (503)** rather than reopened to anonymous traffic. A collector token has **no TTL and is not invalidated by revoking its enrollment**, because a collector is scheduled software rather than a person who has left; revoking stops new tokens being issued. **A Railroad payload is accepted, validated and logged — but the demonstration fleet still generates its signals from physics equations on synthetic traces, so no number in the demo moves because of ingested data.** | Real detector payload schema, defined and versioned with the Railroad |
| 6 | Time source | Host clock, unsynchronized | NTP to Railroad-approved source |
| 7 | Update mechanism | **Partly addressed 2026-11-11.** Deploys are still via git, but a release can now be built reproducibly and signed: `tools/sign_release.py` writes a deterministic archive plus the `MANIFEST.sha256` C01 Part C2 expects, signs it with a detached GPG signature, and verifies against a supplied public key. The release path installs with `--require-hashes`. **What is missing is organisational, not code:** a GPG key must be generated, its custody written, its public half published by a route the Railroad trusts, and `requirements.txt` pinned on a host with index access (`tools/pin_requirements.py`) — until that last step the Docker build **fails by design** rather than installing unpinned | Offline signed update packages with a published key, see D06 and D09 §7.3 |
| 8 | Audit export | **Corrected 2026-11-09, hardened 2026-11-10 and 2026-11-11.** Signed HMAC-SHA256 bundle written by `backend/ledger_export.py`; verified by `tools/verify_ledger_export.py`, which imports nothing from the Platform. Bundles chain via `previous_export_hash` and carry the ledger head so truncation is detectable against a held bundle. Verification requires the bundle to be exactly the four signed parts — an added top-level field is rejected with `bundle_no_extras`, and duplicate JSON keys are refused outright. **2026-11-11: `history_continues` now catches a rewritten history against a held bundle, which `no_truncation` alone did not.** 48 adversarial tests | Built — but see the trust-anchor item below, and read §4.5a on the one-record scope of `history_continues` |
| 9 | Repo hygiene | `axiom.db` and `__pycache__` were committed | Corrected; `.gitignore` added |
| 10 | TLS on the box | Plain HTTP | TLS or network isolation; Railroad's internal standard |
| 11 | **Export signing key provenance** | The key is an operator-held 32-byte secret with a printed `key_id`; its authenticity rests on a written custody procedure, not on a signature from a trusted issuer. The signature is symmetric, so any verifier can also forge | AD-2: bind the key to an issued certification record, or replace HMAC with an asymmetric signature and a published public key |
| 12 | **Off-box replication** | **Partly closed 2026-11-10.** `backend/ledger_replication.py` now produces the D09 §4.5.4 series on a cadence — monthly full, weekly incremental, each bundle chained to the previous by `previous_export_hash`, zero-record weeks kept, nothing overwritten — and its `inspect` verifies each bundle against the one before it and flags a missing period. What it does **not** do is move anything off the box, deliberately: D09 §3.2 promises the Platform has no outbound network, so carrying the series away is the Railroad's physical step under §3.3. Until that step happens a lost disk still loses the ledger, and a missed run is *visible* in the series rather than prevented by it | Scheduled export to a second host, with the receipt acknowledged per D09 §4.4 |

Items 1 and 5 are **blocking** — the certification and detection claims cannot be made until they close. **Item 5's endpoint authentication closed 2026-11-11,** leaving the real payload schema as its only open part. **Item 1's entry half closed 2026-11-11:** a disposition now requires a live session token, and the reviewer identity on the row comes from that session rather than from the request. What keeps the item open is not the software's behaviour but the human process behind a credential — key custody and joiner/mover/leaver — which no amount of code settles; that process is now **written** (D09 §8.4) and is therefore auditable under §10.1, but writing it does not put a named person at the keyboard. The signed key directory is now built, and the item's last column records what it does and does not prove. Authenticating a credential holder is not authenticating a person, and this document does not claim it is. Items 3, 4, 6, 7, 11 and 12 are required before a production licence, not before a demo. Items 2, 8 and 9 are built. Item 10 is specific to the demonstration host and does not arise where the Platform runs on the Railroad's isolated network.

**Items 2 and 8, closed and what that changes.** The append-only guarantee is enforced by the database rather than by convention, and the export is signed and independently verifiable. Two suites test the two halves adversarially: 17 tests attempt an `UPDATE`, a `DELETE`, a second disposition, a tampered row and a removed row against the ledger, and 43 tests attempt to truncate, erase, extend, re-sign, reorder, re-key, wholly rewrite a bundle, and smuggle an unsigned field into one. A third suite of 58 tests attacks the attribution path: an attestation lifted onto another row, an attestation made under an unregistered, revoked, mismatched-reviewer or mismatched-certificate key, a registration date shifted, a registry entry edited or replaced, a manifest that miscounts what it carries, and a parity check that both verifiers catch the same seven structural tampers after the bundle is re-signed. **That suite was then handed to a separate agent whose instruction was to falsify the claim rather than review the code**, and it found a defect the whole suite had missed: the `reviewer` label in an exported attestation was not covered by the HMAC at all, so a holder of any registered reviewer key could relabel another reviewer's row and both verifiers returned a pass. It is fixed — the verifier must now be told which reviewer a key belongs to — and the reason it existed is §4.5a. **The erasure tests exist because the first version of this export passed a total wipe** — every row deleted, an honest empty bundle, a clean verification — and only an independent audit caught it. What remains open has moved from *"there is no signature"* to *"the signature cannot name the export signer, cannot date itself, and cannot detect a first-export-after-wipe"* — item 11, item 12 and the custody procedure. **Per-disposition attribution no longer belongs on that list**: a bundle can now say which registered reviewer attested a row.

87	
88	### E. Forms — the executable instruments
89	
90	Contracts say what the rules are. **Forms are how the rules are actually applied, one event at a time.** Every form is one purpose, one signatory, one stated consequence for silence.
91	
92	| ID | Form | Status | Purpose |
93	|---|---|---|---|
94	| **F00** | Forms Register & Documentation Policy | **Built** | The index, the seven documentation rules, and the rule that governs the others: *if no form exists for what you are about to do, create the form first.* Rule 7 separates a fill-in blank from an unmade decision. |
95	| **F01** | Site Readiness & Survey Questionnaire | **Built** | Pre-deployment site assessment: detector, compute, network, people, existing systems. |
96	| **F02** | Configuration Attestation | **Built** | The Customer's IT Director certifies the installation. **Establishes the Commissioning Date and starts the pilot clock.** The single most important form in the docket. |
97	| **F03** | Change Order | **Built** | The only mechanism by which scope, price or schedule may change on an executed Order. 8-hour tolerance for minor change. |
98	| **F04** | Travel Pre-Approval Request | **Built** | Written approval before any billable travel. Records what we will and will not do on site. |
99	| **F05** | Payment Terms Schedule | **Built** | What is paid, when, and how. Includes the invoicing-discipline rules and the non-suspension commitment. |
100	| **F06** | Deliverable Acceptance | **Built** | Acceptance, acceptance-with-notes, or specific non-conformity. **Silence past 10 Business Days is acceptance.** |
101	| **F07** | Travel & Expense Claim | **Built** | Reimbursement at actual cost, no markup, with cap reconciliation. |
102	| **F08** | Reviewer Certification Application | **Built** | Application, assessment, certification, and revocation. **Still the authoritative certification record** — the key registry exists (2026-11-11) but F08 is what a key is issued from, and entry is not yet gated on either. |
103	| **F09** | Advisory Disposition Record | **Built** | The human decision, recorded. The most legally significant record the Platform produces. Discloses the append-only gap in Part 7. |
104	| **F10** | Security Incident Notification | **Built** | 72-hour Supplier notice, 24-hour Customer notice, RCA, and regulatory hand-off. |
105	| **F11** | Site Visit Report | **Built** | What we observed, **and what we declined to do.** Part 4 records every boundary event. |
106	| **F12** | Formal Notice | **Built** | Termination, breach, cure, non-renewal, conversion election. Delivery method determines effectiveness. |
107	| **F13** | Data Export & Transition Certificate | **Built** | What the Customer gets when it ends, in specific files, with reconciliation. |
108	
109	---
110	
111	## Part III — Loopholes identified, and current status
112	
113	These are the gaps that most often go wrong in rail technology contracts specifically. Status markers show which are now closed by a built document and which remain open work.
114	
115	### 1. The safety-critical disclaimer paradox — the biggest one
116	
117	**Status: CLOSED** — D12 built. The decision-support framing is now fixed in D12 §§1–2, and D12 §9 makes it controlling over every other document.
118	
119	Our claim is that we prevent derailments. Our inevitable limitation-of-liability clause will say we do not guarantee detection. **Put together, those two statements are a contradiction that a plaintiff's lawyer will find in ten minutes.**
120	
121	The resolution is not to weaken either. It is to define the product precisely: AxiomDynamics is a **decision-support system** that presents a ranked, physics-derived risk assessment to a **qualified human reviewer**. 153	**Status: CLOSED** — D05 built. 90-day conversion election window; 50% pilot licence credit ($90K); three-year price lock (Years 1–3 at 0% increase, Year 4+ capped at 5%/yr); defined exit if declined; Year 1 termination for convenience at 60 days with no penalty.
154	
155	If the pilot converts on day 366 at full production price with no credit for pilot fees, the Railroad's internal ROI calculation changes shape at conversion and the deal dies at the CFO's desk, not the lawyer's. **D05 must specify: pilot fee credit, price protection for the first production term, a conversion window, and a defined outcome if they decline** — including whether they keep any data or reports produced during the pilot.
156	
157	### 6. Certification liability — an unnoticed exposure
158	
159	**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §16. Certification evidences completion of the curriculum and creates no liability for a Certified Reviewer's act or omission; the Railroad is solely responsible for its personnel.
160	
161	C02 certifies the Railroad's personnel. **If we certify someone and they then make a consequential error, are we liable for the certification?** This is a real and commonly-missed exposure in any product that trains its customer's staff. D07 must state that certification evidences competency against our curriculum, not a guarantee of individual performance, and that the Railroad retains employment and supervision responsibility.
162	
163	### 7. The air-gap representation problem
164	
165	**Status: CLOSED** — B05 verified against code: zero outbound calls. D09 §3.2 and D07 §7.1 both state it contractually. The supply-chain controls (dependency pinning, hash verification, SBOM and signed release artefacts) are built as of 2026-11-11 and their **applied** state — a pinned file, a shipped SBOM, an issued key — is tracked in D09 §4.4 and Part VI below rather than papered over.
166	
167	We tell customers "on-premise, air-gap capable." If the product requires *any* outbound network call — licence check, telemetry, update ping — that representation is false, and it is the kind of false that surfaces during a security audit in month three.
168	
169	**B05 must be written by someone looking at the actual code, not the marketing.** Then D07 must match B05 exactly. If we need a licence server, say so and design the offline activation path; do not claim air-gap and then require a phone-home.
170	
171	### 8. Cyber incident notification
172	
173	**Status: CLOSED** — D09 §6. 72-hour Supplier-to-Railroad notification, 24-hour Railroad-to-Supplier for discovered vulnerabilities, defined reportable incident, 30-day root-cause analysis, and joint review. D07 §7.5 carries the same window in the master contract.
174	
175	Rail is now explicitly in scope for transportation-sector cyber risk. D09 must include a **breach notification window** (typically 72 hours), the notification channel, and what constitutes a reportable incident. Absent this, the Railroad's CISO will block the deployment regardless of what procurement agreed.
176	
177	### 9. Personnel security and background checks
178	
179	**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §7.7. Supplier personnel with access to Platform IP are subject to background verification; Supplier personnel require no access to Railroad systems at all, which is the structural answer. Railroad-specific screening on any on-site visit is accommodated.
180	
181	Railroad IT will ask whether our engineers have background checks, and whether they will accept the Railroad's. Especially relevant given federal hazmat and security-sensitive rail requirements.
182	
183	### 10. Export control and sanctions
184	
185	**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §13. Mutual compliance, denied-party confirmation, no encryption beyond OS and standard libraries, no re-export without authorisation.
186	
187	Even a domestic-only deployment can raise export-control questions if any component or engineer is foreign-sourced. Cheap to address in D07, expensive to discover later.
188	
189	### 11. Missing: escrow
190	
191	**Status: CLOSED** — D13 §4. Insolvency-triggered, running-version deposit, operability never ownership.
192	
193	If AxiomDynamics ceases to exist, can the Railroad keep operating? A **source code escrow** agreement (triggered on insolvency or cessation of support) is the standard answer and is often the clause that lets a sole-source vendor be approved at all. Given that this is a company selling to organisations that plan in decades, expect this question.
194	
195	### 12. Transition and exit assistance
196	
197	**Status: CLOSED** — D07 §15.6. On termination for any reason except Railroad's uncured breach, 90 days at no charge: data export, transition assistance, final configuration statement. D09 §5 on retention and deletion.
198	
199	What does the Railroad get on termination — data export format, a defined assistance period, and a prohibition on our retaining copies. Must be specified, not implied.
200

204	
205	To prevent the loophole where a technical annex contradicts the master contract:
206	
207	1. **D07 Comprehensive Master Contract** governs generally.
208	2. **D02 Master Pilot Agreement** governs during the pilot term, where it conflicts with D07.

## Part VI — Known gaps between the docket and the build

These are disclosed rather than hidden, and they are tracked here so the docket cannot drift ahead of the code without someone noticing.

| Gap | Where disclosed | Consequence while open |
|---|---|---|
| **The ingest chain is built; nothing behind it is the Railroad's** — `POST /api/ingest` accepts a payload and applies schema → timestamp → plausibility, refusing with a named reason or holding as suspect; but the schema is a demonstration schema (`axiom-detector-payload/v1`), no accepted reading is scored, and although the endpoint is now authenticated for **collectors** (a name-enrolled bearer token held to its own append-only register, 2026-11-11), a collector credential is not a reviewer credential, so the demonstration still ranks synthetic traces | B01 §7 gap #5 · **B02 §2** · **B03 status block** · `assets/ingest-path-build-2026-11-11.md` | **The largest gap in this table.** Every demonstration number is still a demonstration of the method, not of the Railroad's data — building the validator did not put a Railroad reading behind any number. The endpoint's authentication half **closed 2026-11-11** — a collector now presents a bearer token, the gate runs before the body is read, and an unauthenticated POST writes nothing. One sub-gap remains open and **blocking**: the real payload schema must be agreed with the Railroad. **An unauthenticated ingest route is a data-poisoning route** — which is why the credential was built, not merely specified. |
| **The ledger export signature cannot name the signer, and carriage is physical** — since 2026-11-09 the ledger exports as a signed bundle that a recipient verifies without the Platform, which detects altered/added/removed/reordered records and a ledger that has shrunk since a held bundle; since 2026-11-10 the Platform also *produces* the D09 §4.5.4 series itself (monthly full, weekly incremental, chained and content-verified); since 2026-11-11 **each disposition can carry a verifiable reviewer attestation** from an append-only, hash-chained registry, so the bundle names which registered reviewer attested a row. But the HMAC-SHA256 *export* signature is still symmetric and unnamed, attribution says a key holder signed rather than that a person did — a recipient given no reviewer key cannot tell an honest attestation from a fabricated one — the disposition write path no longer accepts a free-text name — entry requires a session since chat-6 — but a session is not an attestation, so an unattested row is still legitimate, nothing can prove when a bundle was made, a wipe before the first bundle in a series stays undetectable, and **the Platform moves nothing off the box** — D09 §3.2 promises no outbound network, so carriage is the Railroad's physical step under §3.3 | B01 §4.5 · **B01 §4.5a** · B01 §7 items 1 and 11–12 · D09 §4.4 · **D09 §4.5** · **C01 §E2** · **F09 Part 7** · `assets/attribution-build-2026-11-11.md` | Per-disposition attribution is now real; **per-export authorship and an instant in time are still not**. Do not call an export a signed certificate of authorship. An independent adversarial audit found nine defects in the attribution build after its suite was green; the worst let any registered key relabel another reviewer's row and pass both verifiers. Fixed, and each is now a test. |
| Certification registry is **local accounts**; entry gated, **custody process written** | B01 §7 gap #1 · D09 §4.4 · **D09 §8.4** · F08 Part 1 | **Narrowed 2026-11-11.** Entry is gated: a disposition requires a live session token, identity comes from the session and not the body, and a certificate revoked mid-session stops writing. **The custody and joiner/mover/leaver procedure is now written (D09 §8.4)** — issuance, mover, leaver, rotation, the custody log, and the quarterly reconciliation against F08 — with `tools/issue_reviewer_key.py` as the joiner step and the signed key directory built. What remains open is what no procedure closes: a credential holder is not a person, and entry requires a live **session** but still not an **attestation**, so an attested row remains the reviewer's choice rather than the product's requirement. |
| **SBOM: generator built, nothing shipped carrying one** — `tools/sbom.py` produces a CycloneDX 1.5 document from the installed tree with a per-file tree digest and the bundled native libraries, and `verify` recomputes it on the customer's machine. No release has shipped with one attached | D09 §4.4 · **D09 §7.2** · **D10 Part 5** | Customer cannot yet verify the dependency chain from what they were given. Needs a run on the **target architecture**, because the numpy wheel is platform-specific. |
| **Hash pinning: tool built, file not pinned** — `tools/pin_requirements.py` pins to observed index digests and the Dockerfile/release path now pass `--require-hashes`, so an unpinned file **fails the build** rather than shipping with a flag that reads as a control | D09 §4.4 · **D10 Part 5** | A compromised index could serve a substituted file. The pin step needs index access and must be run on the release host; a hand-written digest would be worse than none. |
| **Signed releases: tool built, key not issued** — `tools/sign_release.py` builds a reproducible archive, writes the C01 manifest and signs it with GPG, verifying against a supplied public key | D09 §4.4 · **D09 §7.3** · **D10 Part 5** | A release archive could be substituted in transit until a key exists and its public half reaches the Railroad by a path independent of the archive. |
| **D10 understated the component inventory until 2026-11-11** — it called numpy "one component" and "the complete inventory"; the wheel bundles OpenBLAS, LAPACK, libgfortran (GPL-3.0 + GCC runtime exception), libquadmath (LGPL-2.1), lapack-lite, dragon4 and libdivide | **D10 Part 2** · D09 §7.2 | Corrected. A register that says "one component" when eight libraries execute in-process is the kind of understatement a security reviewer finds and a buyer remembers. |
| Licence scope enforced **by contract only**, not by the software | D02 §6 · D05 §5.2 | Nothing technically prevents a second site. Scope is an obligation, not a control. |
| Insurance limit is **$2M, not $5M** | D07 §10.1 · D03 §9 | Stated honestly with a step-up commitment. Certificates must match the clause. |

**The rule for this table:** a gap moves from here to closed only when the code changes, and the entries in B01, D09, F08 and F09 are amended in the same commit. Documenting a fix that was not made is the exact failure this docket was built to prevent.

**Closed:** the disposition ledger append-only gap (AD-3). Closed 2026-11-09 in the commit that rebuilt `backend/store.py`, added 17 adversarial tests in `tests/test_store.py`, and amended B01 §4 and §7 item 2, D09 §4.4 and the audit-logging row, F09 Parts 6–7 and its footer, and this table. The gap did not disappear — it narrowed. What was open was "a disposition can be silently replaced"; that is now impossible. What remains is "the ledger cannot be proven untampered by a party holding the database file", and that is the row above.

**Also closed, same day:** the *unsigned* half of the row above. `backend/ledger_export.py` now writes a signed bundle and `tools/verify_ledger_export.py` verifies it without importing Platform code, so a party holding only the bundle and the key can confirm no record was altered or removed. The row was rewritten rather than deleted, because the signature introduced limits of its own — it is symmetric, it cannot date itself, and a wipe before the first bundle in a series is invisible to later ones — and a gap table that silently loses a row teaches the next reader to trust it less.

> **One correction worth recording, because this table exists to prevent it.** The first version of the export passed a total wipe: delete every row, export honestly, and a recipient holding the previous bundle was told every check passed. The checks were each individually correct and the set proved nothing, because none compared the bundle against one the recipient already had. Fixed by recording the ledger's own head in each bundle and failing when a later one reports a shorter ledger. That the gap was caught before this table claimed the control closed is the only reason the table is still worth reading.

---

*This docket index is a working structure, not a legal opinion. Every document in Part II under D must be reviewed by qualified counsel in the relevant jurisdiction before execution. Nothing here constitutes legal advice.*

## How to save memories

**Write early, write often.** Memory writes are cheap; rediscovery is expensive. Don't wait for a clean stopping point — there isn't one. Good moments to write include:
- figuring out why something was broken or behaving unexpectedly
- learning a fact, constraint, or config detail that wasn't obvious from the code/docs
- making a non-trivial decision (record the *why*, not just the what)
- discovering that an approach *doesn't* work — negative results save future time too
- finishing a sub-task or switching context
- noticing you've been working >15-20 min without saving anything
- finishing research (even partially)

**Err toward writing.** If you're unsure whether something is worth saving, save it — a slightly noisy memory is far better than an empty one.

Saving a memory is a two-step process:

**Step 1** — write the memory to its own file (e.g., `user_role.md`, `feedback_testing.md`) using this frontmatter format:

```markdown
---
name: {{memory name — other memories can reference this one inline as [[name]]}}
description: {{one-line description — used to decide relevance in future conversations, so be specific}}
type: {{user, feedback, project, reference}}
---

{{memory content — for feedback/project types, structure as: rule/fact, then **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Use [[name]] to reference other memories by their name field. [[name]] should match filename.}}
```

**Step 2** — add a pointer to that file in `MEMORY.md`. `MEMORY.md` is an index, not a memory — each entry should be one line, under ~150 characters: `- [Title](file.md) — one-line hook`. It has no frontmatter. Never write memory content directly into `MEMORY.md`.

- `MEMORY.md` is the index and, when there is one, is loaded into your conversation context — lines after 200 will be truncated, so keep the index concise. If no index is loaded, `MEMORY.md` was missing or empty when this conversation started.
- Keep the name, description, and type fields in memory files up-to-date with the content
- Organize memory semantically by topic, not chronologically
- Update or remove memories that turn out to be wrong or outdated
- Do not write duplicate memories. First check if there is an existing memory you can update before writing a new one.
